paper_metadata.title: Continuous-Variable Quantum K-Means Clustering With Photonic Gaussian States

summary: The paper presents a continuous-variable photonic K-means implementation using Strawberry Fields on Xanadu hardware and evaluates it on IRIS (150 instances, 4 features, 3 clusters), Wine (178, 13, 3), and a synthetic dataset (200, 5, 4). Reported CVQK-means accuracies are 88.67%, 70.22%, and 84.5%, with SSD values 74.2, 2.37×10^6, and 936.55, respectively, which are comparable to classical K-means rather than better.

experiments.description: Continuous-variable quantum K-means clustering on photonic Gaussian states, evaluated on IRIS, Wine, and a synthetic dataset and compared against classical K-means.

algorithm.variant: Continuous-Variable Quantum K-Means (CVQK-Means) with Gaussian states
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterate assignment/update steps until centroids converge or maximum number of iterations is reached

hyperparameters.encoding: Gaussian-state encoding with displacement and fixed squeezing

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initialize centroids as continuous-variable quantum states; specific parameter values not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Classical data points are encoded into continuous-variable Gaussian states using displacement and squeezing operations; centroids are also represented as CV quantum states
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize within-cluster variance / sum of squared distances, analogous to classical K-means

problem_instance.description: Unsupervised clustering of benchmark datasets using CV quantum photonic hardware

dataset_specification.description: IRIS: 150 instances, 4 features, 3 clusters; Wine: 178 instances, 13 features, 3 clusters; Synthetic: 200 instances, 5 features, 4 clusters

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical data encoded into quadrature variables of Gaussian states; no further preprocessing details reported
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compared clustering accuracy and sum of squared distances (SSD) against classical K-means on the same datasets

noise_model.noise_type: quantum noise in photonic hardware (not quantified)
noise_model.error_mitigation_method: None reported; discussion mentions possible future use of GKP code and noise-adaptive averaging

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Data encoded into Gaussian states via displacement and squeezing
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Cluster labels and centroids extracted; accuracy and SSD computed

speedup_claims.conditions: Empirical comparison on IRIS, Wine, and Synthetic datasets using continuous-variable photonic quantum hardware
speedup_claims.caveats: No asymptotic or runtime speedup is claimed; the paper reports comparable clustering accuracy and SSD only.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not established; the paper reports only empirical clustering accuracy and SSD on three small benchmark datasets, with no runtime, asymptotic complexity, or scaling evidence.
limiting_factors: No demonstrated speedup over classical K-means
Continuous-variable photonic implementation lacks reported resource counts

notes: Paper explicitly reports implementation on Xanadu photonic hardware via Strawberry Fields, but does not specify a device name or qubit count; CV photonic setting means qubit count is not applicable/not reported.
No circuit depth, gate counts, shots, or variational parameters are reported because the algorithm is described in continuous-variable Gaussian-state terms rather than a discrete gate-count circuit.
No asymptotic speedup claim is characterized; results are empirical comparisons to classical K-means only.
The paper reports comparable performance to classical K-means on IRIS, Wine, and Synthetic datasets, but does not claim a practical quantum advantage.
